nodes.name: Transformer as interacting particle system; empirical measure
nodes.statement_short: Transformers viewed as an interacting particle system of tokens on the sphere driven by the empirical measure $\mu(t)$.

nodes.name: Interacting particle system (Transformer dynamics)
nodes.statement: \dot{x}_i(t) = v[\mu(t)](t,x_i(t)) \hspace{1cm} \text{ for } t\in[0,T],
nodes.label: eq: ips

nodes.name: Transformer vector field and self-attention
nodes.statement_short: The velocity field combines self-attention (softmax-weighted average) and a ReLU perceptron, projected on the tangent space.

nodes.name: Transformer vector field
nodes.statement: v[\mu](t,x) = \bm{\mathsf{P}}^\perp_{x}\left(\bm{\mathit{V}}(t)\mathscr{A}_{\bm{\mathit{B}}}[\mu](t,x)+\bm{\mathit{W}}(t)\big(\bm{\mathit{U}}(t)x+b(t)\big)_+\right)
nodes.label: eq: vf

nodes.name: Self-attention mechanism
nodes.statement: \mathscr{A}_{\bm{\mathit{B}}}[\mu](t,x) := \dfrac{\displaystyle\int e^{\langle \bm{\mathit{B}}(t)x, x'\rangle}x'\mu(\, \mathrm{d} x')}{\displaystyle\int e^{\langle \bm{\mathit{B}}(t)x, \zeta\rangle}\mu(\, \mathrm{d}\zeta)}.
nodes.label: eq: attention

nodes.name: Transformer parameters
nodes.statement: The parameters $\bm{\mathit{V}}(t),\bm{\mathit{B}}(t),\bm{\mathit{W}}(t),\bm{\mathit{U}}(t)$, which are all $d\times d$ matrices, and $b(t)$, which is a $d$-dimensional vector, are to be used to steer the flow to one's liking.

nodes.name: Perceptron and layer normalization
nodes.statement:
The vector field $v[\mu(t)](t,\cdot)$ is a combination of the self-attention mechanism $\mathscr{A}_{\bm{\mathit{B}}}[\mu(t)](t,\cdot)$ and a \emph{perceptron}


at every layer $t$, ultimately projected onto $\mathsf{T}_x\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ by virtue of the orthogonal projector $\bm{\mathsf{P}}^\perp_x:= I_d-xx^\top$, referred to as \emph{layer normalization}.
nodes.statement_short: Layer normalization is the tangent projector $I_d-xx^\top$ applied to the attention-plus-perceptron field.

nodes.name: Transformer as solution map of the continuity equation
nodes.statement_short: The Transformer is the solution map of the nonlinear continuity equation driven by $v[\mu]$.

nodes.name: Continuity equation Cauchy problem
nodes.label: eq: cauchy.pb

nodes.name: Measure-to-measure matching (ensemble transportation) problem
nodes.statement_short: Given N input-target pairs of probability measures on the sphere, find one set of parameters whose flow maps each input to its target.

nodes.name: Ensemble transportation / controllability with a single control
nodes.statement: This is an \emph{ensemble transportation} or \emph{controllability} problem, since we seek to accomplish this matching of measures by means of the flow of \eqref{eq: cauchy.pb} for a \emph{single} parameter or control $\theta=(\bm{\mathit{W}}(t),\bm{\mathit{V}}(t),\bm{\mathit{B}}(t),\bm{\mathit{U}}(t), b(t))_{t\in[0,T]}$.

nodes.name: Proof sketch of the main theorem
nodes.statement_short: Compose three flows: disentangle inputs and targets with attention, then match the disentangled measures with clustering and perceptron flows, and invert the target flow.

nodes.name: Three-flow decomposition
nodes.statement_short: Write the final map as a composition of three flows.

nodes.name: Disentangle the inputs
nodes.statement:
$\Phi_{\theta_1}^t:\mathscr{P}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})\to\mathscr{P}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})$ is the solution map of \eqref{eq: cauchy.pb} on $[0,\frac{T}{3}]$, generated by piecewise constant parameters $\theta_1$ 
, having $O(d\cdot N)$ switches, as to disentangle the supports of the input measures (the use of the attention component is \emph{necessary} for this step). After this step, the supports of the measures are disjoint:
\begin{equation} \mathrm{supp}\left(\Phi_{\theta_1}^{\frac{T}{3}}(\mu_0^i)\right)\cap\mathrm{supp}\left(\Phi_{\theta_1}^{\frac{T}{3}}(\mu_0^j)\right)=\varnothing\quad\text{ whenever }i\neq j.
\end{equation}
This is done in \Cref{prop: separation} in {\bf \Cref{sec: disentanglement}}.
The clue lies in following the insights of \cite{geshkovski2023mathematical}, which entail clustering of every individual measure to a single point mass in long time in the special regime $\bm{\mathit{B}}=\beta I_d$ with $\beta\geqslant 0$ and $\bm{\mathit{V}}=I_d$. Should the limit point masses corresponding to every input measure be located at different positions, the disentanglement property \eqref{eq: disentanglement.intro} would readily follow by taking the time horizon $T$ large enough. Unfortunately, characterizing the location of the limit point mass for general measures is an open problem. 
We instead consider a curated choice of $\bm{\mathit{V}}$ to facilitate locating the limiting cluster for every measure, which we now sketch. Consider $N=2$ (the general case is argued by induction; see \Cref{lem: induction.barycenter}) and suppose that $\mathbb{E}_{\mu_0^1}[z]$ and $\mathbb{E}_{\mu_0^2}[z]$ are not colinear (this assumption is not needed, as seen in \Cref{lem: colinearity}). 

We can take $\bm{\mathit{B}}\equiv0$ (we provide an alternative proof when $\bm{\mathit{B}}\not\equiv0$ in {\bf \Cref{sec: beyond.the.average}}) and 
\begin{equation*}
    \bm{\mathit{V}}(t) := \sum_{k=1}^{d-1} \alpha_k\alpha_k^\top 1_{[T_k,T_{k+1}]}(t),
\end{equation*}
where $\{\alpha_k\}$ is an orthonormal basis of $(\text{span}\,\mathbb{E}_{\mu_0^1}[z])^\perp$. Then there is some index $\ell$ such that $\langle \mathbb{E}_{\mu_0^1}[z], \alpha_\ell\rangle=0$ and $\langle \mathbb{E}_{\mu_0^2}[z], \alpha_\ell\rangle\neq 0$. Consequently the quantity $t\mapsto\langle \mathbb{E}_{\mu^i(t)}[z], \alpha_\ell\rangle$ remains constant when $i=1$, and does not change sign when $i=2$. After an elementary computation one can then see that any $x(t)\in\mathrm{supp}(\mu^2(t))$ converges to $\pm\alpha_\ell$ in long time, whereas $\mu^1(t)=\mu_0^1$ throughout. One can always rescale time so that the above holds at an arbitrary prescribed horizon, at the cost of increasing the norm of the parameters.
nodes.statement_short: First flow disentangles input supports via attention along a basis orthogonal to one barycenter.

nodes.name: Disentanglement of supports
nodes.statement: \mathrm{supp}\left(\Phi_{\theta_1}^{\frac{T}{3}}(\mu_0^i)\right)\cap\mathrm{supp}\left(\Phi_{\theta_1}^{\frac{T}{3}}(\mu_0^j)\right)=\varnothing\quad\text{ whenever }i\neq j.
nodes.label: eq: disentanglement.intro

nodes.name: Location of the limit cluster for general measures
nodes.statement: Unfortunately, characterizing the location of the limit point mass for general measures is an open problem.

nodes.name: Disentangle the targets
nodes.statement:
In the same vein, $\Phi_{\theta_3}^t:\mathscr{P}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})\to\mathscr{P}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})$ is the solution map of \eqref{eq: cauchy.pb} on $[\frac{2T}{3}, T]$, 
generated by piecewise constant parameters $\theta_3,$ 
 as to disentangle the supports of the target measures:
\begin{equation*}
\mathrm{supp}\left(\Phi_{\theta_3}^{\frac{T}{3}}(\mu_1^i)\right)\cap\mathrm{supp}\left(\Phi_{\theta_3}^{\frac{T}{3}}(\mu_1^j)\right)=\varnothing\quad\text{ whenever }i\neq j.
\end{equation*}
Inverting $\Phi_{\theta_3}^t$ simply corresponds to running time backwards from $T$ to $\frac{2T}{3}$.
nodes.statement_short: Third flow disentangles target supports and is inverted.

nodes.name: Match disentangled measures
nodes.statement_short: Middle flow matches disentangled inputs to disentangled targets by clustering and point matching or map approximation.

nodes.name: Linear continuity equations cannot match general ensembles
nodes.statement: Matching general ensembles of measures \emph{cannot} be done with a single \emph{linear} continuity equation, as is done in the Benamou-Brenier reformulation of optimal transport for instance \cite{benamou2000computational}, namely \eqref{eq: cauchy.pb} in which the vector field $v$ does not depend on $\mu(t)$.
nodes.statement_short: A measure-independent (linear) continuity equation cannot map overlapping inputs to disjoint targets.
conclusions: Matching general ensembles of measures \emph{cannot} be done with a single \emph{linear} continuity equation

nodes.name: Counterexample for linear continuity equations
nodes.statement:
Indeed, take for instance $\mu_0^1,\mu_0^2\in\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{ac}}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})$ such that 
$$\mathrm{supp}(\mu_0^1)\cap \mathrm{supp}(\mu_0^2)\neq\varnothing,$$
and similarly $\mu_1^1,\mu_1^2\in \mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{ac}}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})$ such that
\begin{equation} \mathrm{supp}(\mu_1^1)\cap \mathrm{supp}(\mu_1^2)=\varnothing.
\end{equation}
Then there cannot exist a single-valued $\mathsf{T}:\mathbb{S}^{d-1}\to\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ such that $\mathsf{T}_\#\mu_0^1=\mu_1^1$ and $\mathsf{T}_\#\mu_0^2=\mu_1^2$, since there would have to exist $x\in \mathrm{supp}(\mu_0^1)\cap \mathrm{supp}(\mu_0^2)$ for which $\mathsf{T}(x)$ would have to take two different values due to \eqref{eq: empty.intersection}.
nodes.statement_short: Counterexample: a single-valued map cannot send a common support point to two disjoint target supports.

nodes.name: Disjoint target supports
nodes.statement: \mathrm{supp}(\mu_1^1)\cap \mathrm{supp}(\mu_1^2)=\varnothing.
nodes.label: eq: empty.intersection

nodes.name: Why d >= 3 is required
nodes.statement: The requirement $d \geqslant 3$ in \Cref{thm: main.result} stems from matching disentangled measures. In $d = 2$, the problem becomes intrinsically one-dimensional, and in such a setting, the order of particles is preserved. This obstruction impedes the conclusion of the disentanglement. To carry through our strategy, one needs to use self-attention to order the input measures and disentangle them.

nodes.name: Transport-map assumption is minimal
nodes.statement: When the targets are more general than point masses---as in \Cref{thm: main.result}---we operate under the assumption that there exists a transport map between every pair $(\mu_0^i, \mu_1^i)$. This is again satisfied for many cases of interest; for instance, whenever $\mu_0^i$ is absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ (per the celebrated theorem(s) of Brenier-McCann \cite{brenier1991polar, mccann2001polar}), or whenever $\mu_0^i$ and $\mu_1^i$ are empirical measures with $\mu_0^i$ having as many atoms as $\mu_1^i$. This assumption is also minimal. Indeed, since $v[\mu(t)](t,\cdot)$ is Lipschitz, any solution to \eqref{eq: cauchy.pb} can be written as the image measure of the initial data by means of some map. This presents a natural impediment to matching a measure constituted by a single atom to a measure with two atoms.
nodes.statement_short: Existence of transport maps holds e.g. for absolutely continuous inputs (Brenier-McCann) and is necessary since flows are Lipschitz.

nodes.name: Mismatched numbers of atoms
nodes.statement:
If the input $\mu_0^i$ and output $\mu_1^i$ are empirical measures having $n$ and $m$ atoms respectively, 
    with $n > m$ and $\frac{n}{m} \notin \mathbb{N}$, then there does not exist a transport map between $\mu_0^i$ and $\mu_1^ i$. 
    Consequently, for the same reason as in the previous point, it is not possible to find a solution to \eqref{eq: cauchy.pb} that approximates $\mu_1^i$ to any desired level of accuracy. However, if to each atom of $\mu_1^i$ one assigns  $\lfloor n/m \rfloor$ atoms of $\mu_0^i$, then one can construct a map $\mathsf{T}^i$ such that $\mathsf{W}_2(\mathsf{T}_\#^i\mu_0^i, \mu_1^i) = O\left(m/n\right)$. As a result, we could use the flow map of  \eqref{eq: cauchy.pb} to approximate all $N$ target measures 
     to error $O(\varepsilon+m/n)$.
nodes.statement_short: With n input and m target atoms and n/m not an integer no transport map exists, but matching up to $O(\varepsilon+m/n)$ is possible.

nodes.name: Exact matching of empirical measures
nodes.statement: We can exactly match $N$ empirical input measures to $N$ empirical target measures as long as they have the same number of atoms.
assumptions: as long as they have the same number of atoms
conclusions: We can exactly match $N$ empirical input measures to $N$ empirical target measures

nodes.name: Exact matching via the proof of the main theorem
nodes.statement: This follows as a corollary of the proof of \Cref{thm: main.result}, since no quantization is required in \Cref{lem: univ.approx}.
nodes.statement_short: Corollary of the main proof: no quantization is needed in the approximation lemma for atomic measures.

nodes.name: Obstructions to exact matching
nodes.statement: Since $v[\mu(t)](t,\cdot)$ is Lipschitz, we cannot do exact transportation of an absolutely continuous measure to a discrete one even when $N=1$. Similarly, we cannot match a single input measure with connected support to a target measure whose support has multiple connected components.

nodes.name: Beyond W2: Kullback-Leibler approximation
nodes.statement:
We opted for approximation in the Wasserstein distance because working with distances is convenient. The result could be adapted to encompass the Kullback-Leibler divergence  $(\mathsf{KL})$, which is the natural candidate in view of applications.

(Note that this would be a stronger approximation result by virtue of \cite{bolley2005weighted}, which only requires the second argument in the $\mathsf{KL}$ to have a Gaussian moment, guaranteed in our case by working on $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$.)


To achieve this, after the step involving the disentanglement of supports, we can match the disentangled measures approximately in $\mathsf{TV}$ instead of $\mathsf{W}_2$ by following a similar approach to the one developed in \cite{ruiz2024control}, and then apply a reverse Pinsker inequality \cite[Theorem 7]{verdu2014total} (see also \cite{sason2016f}). However, to do so, one needs that the measures are mutually absolutely continuous and to have a bounded likelihood ratio. 




This approach would avoid quantizing the (disentangled) target measure and thus clustering the (disentangled) inputs into atoms.
nodes.statement_short: The result could be adapted to KL via TV matching and a reverse Pinsker inequality, given bounded likelihood ratios.

nodes.name: Decomposition of the number of switches
nodes.section: 1.4.3 On the number of parameter switches

nodes.name: Switches for point-mass targets
nodes.statement:
In \Cref{thm: targets.atoms}, once the input measures are rendered disentangled, we use a single constant parameter that results in clustering over time (as per \cite{geshkovski2023mathematical}), collapsing each input measure to a point mass. Thus, 
    $$\#\text{switches}_{\text{clustering}}=0.$$
    The resulting ensemble of point masses can then be matched to the targets using the perceptron component (adapting ideas from \cite{ruiz2023neural, li2022deep}) with 
    $$\#\text{switches}_{\text{matching}}=O(N).$$
    So the switches in \Cref{thm: targets.atoms} arise primarily from the disentangling step. In particular, if the source measures have disjoint support, then the number of switches becomes $O(N)$ which is dimension independent.
nodes.section: 1.4.3 On the number of parameter switches

nodes.name: Switches for absolutely continuous inputs and empirical targets
nodes.statement:
Consider \Cref{thm: main.result}, with targets that are empirical measures having $m \geqslant 2$ atoms, and inputs that are all absolutely continuous. As seen in \Cref{proof: proof.restricted} (restricted case), the proof can be significantly simplified in this case. Indeed, one can avoid a direct application of \Cref{lem: univ.approx} and \Cref{prop: compression} by instead iteratively applying \Cref{lem: two.balls}
    to each input measure. Namely, after the disentanglement step (with a sufficiently large separation), we partition the support of each disentangled input measure into $m$ pieces, which we can cluster to a point with a single constant parameter per piece using \Cref{lem: two.balls}. All in all, 
    $$\#\text{switches}_{\text{clustering}} = O(m\cdot N).$$
    The resulting clustered measures can then be matched to the empirical target measures by \Cref{prop: interpolation.neural.ode} at the cost of 
    $$\#\text{switches}_{\text{matching}} = O(m \cdot N).$$  
    All in all,
    $$
    \#\mathrm{switches} = O\big((m+d)N\big).
    $$
nodes.section: 1.4.3 On the number of parameter switches

nodes.name: Switches for empirical inputs and targets
nodes.statement:
Suppose both the inputs and targets are empirical measures, with $n$ and $m$ atoms, respectively. 
    When it comes to $\#\text{switches}_{\text{clustering}}$, if $n \gg m$ or $m$ is a divisor of $n$, one can use $m$ balls per measure in \Cref{prop: compression} instead of packing, which would lead to 
    $$\#\text{switches}_{\text{clustering}} = O(m \cdot N).$$ 
    To achieve this, one can combine \Cref{prop: separation} with the clustering of measures to a point mass as in \Cref{prop: targets.atoms}, much like what is done in the \Cref{proof: proof.restricted} (restricted case). 
    By virtue of the latter, we can partition the support of each measure using large balls that are not necessarily contained within the support. All in all,
    $$
    \#\mathrm{switches} = O\big((m+d)N\big).
    $$
    
    To put things into context: in the discrete-time setting of \cite{yun2019transformers}, while the number of layers is seemingly independent of the number of sequences $N$, it is exponential in the dimension $d$.
nodes.section: 1.4.3 On the number of parameter switches

nodes.name: Clustering switches for general targets
nodes.statement: In the case of general target measures as in \Cref{thm: main.result}, $\#\text{switches}_{\text{clustering}}$ is exponential in the dimension $d$ due to the use of a specific strategy which leverages packing numbers---see \Cref{rem: nb.disc.clustering}.
nodes.section: 1.4.3 On the number of parameter switches

nodes.name: Increasing the width
nodes.statement: {\bf Increasing the width.} Many of the actions used throughout our proofs are performed using the perceptron component with constant parameter matrices $\bm{\mathit{W}}$ and $\bm{\mathit{U}}$ that are of rank 1. One could, of course, consider using rectangular matrices instead, thus increasing the \emph{width} of the network, which could, in turn, reduce the number of switches ($\approx$ depth).

nodes.name: Multi-head attention
nodes.statement:
{\bf Multi-head attention.} The computation of token similarities through self-attention is typically parallelized in practice throughout several \emph{heads}, lending way to \emph{multi-head self-attention}. This boils down to replacing the term 
    $$\bm{\mathit{V}}(t)\mathscr{A}_{\bm{\mathit{B}}}[\mu(t)](t,x)$$ 
    in \eqref{eq: vf} by
    \begin{equation*}
        \sum_{h=1}^H \bm{\mathit{V}}_h(t)\mathscr{A}_{\bm{\mathit{B}}_h}[\mu(t)](t,x).
    \end{equation*}
    We now dispose of $H\geqslant1$ parameters $(\bm{\mathit{V}}_h(t),\bm{\mathit{B}}_h(t))_{h\in[H]}$ at every time $t$. We do not know how to exploit multiple heads in our proofs, although some theoretical insights thereon can be found in the proofs in \cite{chen2024provably}.
nodes.statement_short: Multi-head attention replaces $V A_B$ by a sum over heads; the proofs do not exploit multiple heads.

nodes.name: Discrete-time Transformers
nodes.statement: {\bf Discrete time.} The continuous-time formulation gives rise to an equation that is \emph{reversible in time}, which we often use in our construction. In particular, the task of disentangling supports becomes equivalent to the task of entangling supports, which is not the case in the non-reversible scenario. Our results are expected to hold for an appropriate discretization of \eqref{eq: cauchy.pb} with a sufficiently small time step.

nodes.name: Beyond the ReLU perceptron
nodes.statement: {\bf Beyond the ReLU perceptron.} All of our results remain unchanged if one replaces $(\cdot)_+$ (the ReLU) by any other Lipschitz nonlinearity that equals the ReLU near the origin. It is likely that the proofs can be generalized to even encompass the hyperbolic tangent. The relevant property that the nonlinear activation function ought to satisfy is to ensure that the resulting  flow (when $\bm{\mathit{V}}\equiv0$) leaves any spherical cap of choice invariant.

nodes.name: Integration and gradient conventions
nodes.statement: Unless stated otherwise, all integrals are taken over $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$, and all $\nabla$ denote the spherical gradient.

nodes.name: Index set [n] and lesssim
nodes.statement: We use $[n]:=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, and $f(x) \lesssim g(x)$ if there exists a finite positive constant $C$ such that $f(x) \leqslant Cg(x)$.

nodes.name: lesssim_S
nodes.statement: We write $f(x) \lesssim_S g(x)$ if the resulting constant depends on $S$.

nodes.name: Geodesic distance on the sphere
nodes.statement: We denote by $d_g(x,y)$ the geodesic distance between $x, y \in \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$, which, as a reminder, is the great-circle distance $d_g(x,y) = \arccos(\langle x, y \rangle)$.

nodes.name: Convex hull and geodesic convex hull
nodes.statement: For $A \subset \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$, we denote by $\mathrm{conv}\, A$ the convex hull of $A$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$, and by $\mathrm{conv}_g\, A$ the geodesic convex hull of $A$ in $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ (the smallest geodesically convex set containing $A$).

nodes.name: Wasserstein-p distance
nodes.statement:

nodes.name: Geodesic
nodes.statement: A geodesic is a smooth curve with zero acceleration, namely, a smooth \( \gamma: I \to \mathbb{S}^{d-1} \) with \( \bm{\mathsf{P}}^\perp_{\gamma(t)}(\ddot{\gamma}(t)) = 0 \) for \( t \in I \), where \( I \) is an open interval.

nodes.name: Geodesics lie on great circles
nodes.statement:
Geodesics on \( \mathbb{S}^{d-1} \) lie on great circles, specifically, there exists \( v \in \mathbb{S}^{d-1} \) such that
\[
\gamma(t) \subset \{x \in \mathbb{S}^{d-1} : \langle x, v \rangle = 0 \}\,, \quad \forall\, t \in I\,.
\]
conclusions: Geodesics on \( \mathbb{S}^{d-1} \) lie on great circles

nodes.name: Minimizing geodesic
nodes.statement: Given two points \( x, y \in \mathbb{S}^{d-1} \), a geodesic \( \gamma: [a,b] \to \mathbb{S}^{d-1} \) is called a minimal or minimizing geodesic between \( x \) and \( y \) if \( \gamma \) is of speed 1 (i.e., \( \|\dot{\gamma}(t)\| = 1 \)), satisfies \( \gamma(a) = x \) and \( \gamma(b) = y \), and \( d_g(x,y) = b - a \).

nodes.name: Uniqueness of minimizing geodesics
nodes.statement: If \( x \) and \( y \) are not antipodal, the minimizing geodesic between them is unique and is simply the segment between them on the great circle on which they both lie.
assumptions: If \( x \) and \( y \) are not antipodal
conclusions: the minimizing geodesic between them is unique and is simply the segment between them on the great circle on which they both lie

nodes.name: Convergence along all times
nodes.statement:
Therefore, we found a sequence of positive times $\{T_n\}_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ with $T_n=T_{\varepsilon_{1,n}}+T_{\frac{\varepsilon}{3}}$ for which $\mu_n=\mu(T_n)$ converges to $\delta_{x^*}$ in $\mathsf{W}_\infty$. Thanks to  \eqref{eq: set.inclusion}, the convergence does not depend on the sequence of times. Indeed, for every $t\geqslant T_n$, we have
\begin{align*}
    \mathsf{W}_\infty(\mu(t),\delta_{x^*})\leqslant\max_{y\in \mathrm{conv}_g\mathrm{supp}(\mu(t))}d_g(y,x^*)&\leqslant \max_{y\in \mathrm{conv}_g\mathrm{supp}(\mu_n)}d_g(y,x^*)\\
    &\leqslant\max_{y\in B(x^*,\mathsf{W}_\infty(\mu_n,\delta_{x^*}))}d_g(y,x^*)\\
    &=2\mathsf{W}_\infty(\mu_n,\delta_{x^*})\\
    &\leqslant 2\varepsilon
\end{align*}
where $B_n\coloneqq B(x^*,\mathsf{W}_\infty(\mu_n,\delta_{x^*}))$ is the ball on $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ centered at $x^*$ with radius $\mathsf{W}_\infty(\mu_n,\delta_{x^*})$. As $B_n$ is geodesically convex, and since $\mathrm{supp}(\mu_n)\subset B_n$, one has  $\mathrm{conv}_g\mathrm{supp}(\mu_n)\subset B_n$.

The cases $d>3$ follow by repeating the above argument.

\end{equation*}
where $x(\cdot)$ is the solution to the Cauchy problem for \eqref{eq: neural.ode.separation} with data $x_0$. 
Since $\|\gamma\|=1$, $\|\bm{\mathit{W}}_1\|_{\text{op}}\leqslant1$ and $\|b_1\|\leqslant\frac{\epsilon}{2}\sqrt{d}$, bounding the $L^\infty$--norm of the parameters comes from bounding $T_{\frac{\pi}{16}}(x_0)$ uniformly over $x_0\in\mathscr{S}_+$ and rescaling time. 
For every $x_0\in B\left(\omega_+,\frac{\pi}{16}\right)$ we see that $T_{\frac{\pi}{16}}(x_0)$ is trivially $0$, whereas for  $x_0\in \mathscr{S}_+\setminus B\left(\omega_+,\frac{\pi}{16}\right)$ one has
\begin{align} \frac{\, \mathrm{d}}{\, \mathrm{d} t} \langle x(t),\omega_+\rangle&=\left( \langle \gamma, x(t)\rangle-\frac{\epsilon}{2}\right)_+\left(1-\langle \omega_+,x\rangle^2\right)\nonumber\\
&\geqslant \frac{\epsilon}{2}\left(1-\langle \omega_+,x\rangle^2\right)\nonumber\\
&\geqslant \frac{\epsilon}{2}\left(1-\cos^2\left(\frac{\pi}{16}\right)\right).
\end{align}
Hence $T_{\frac{\pi}{16}}(x_0)=O(1/\epsilon)$ for all $x_0\in \mathscr{S}_+$.

nodes.name: Differences with GPT-2
nodes.statement:
Our model is not exactly the same as the one used in {\sf GPT-2}, as it differs in two ways: 
\begin{itemize}
\item We focus on \emph{encoder} models, namely those in which  self-attention is defined as in \eqref{eq: attention}. Models such as {\sf GPT} are \emph{decoder} models: they are causal as they use a masked self-attention mechanism. 
These models are not addressed herein. It is worth noting that the equation is remarkably similar, and the probability flow interpretation persists---see \cite{castin2023understanding}.

\item We use \emph{post-layer normalization}, instead of \emph{pre-layer normalization} as done in \Cref{fig: gpt}, which consists in simply permuting the order of the {\tt norm} and {\tt attn}, and {\tt norm} and {\tt mlp} operations. This is a minor modeling detail.

nodes.statement: \left(\Phi_{\eta\#} \nu_0^i\right)(\mathbb{Q}_1^{d-1})=1-\eta

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma B.1
nodes.statement_short: Move the mass outside the orthant to a single atom inside it.

nodes.name: Removing the hole assumption
nodes.statement:
\Cref{lem: first.quadrant} provides a map $\Phi_\eta$ that ensures \eqref{eq: mass.first.quadrant}. 
By virtue of \Cref{lem: mass.concentration.Q1}, we can extend \Cref{thm: main.result} to the setting of measures whose support fill $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$, namely, the assumption of having a point $\omega\notin\bigcup_{i}\mathrm{supp}(\mu_0^i)$ can be removed.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 1.2 extends to measures whose supports fill the sphere.
conclusions: we can extend \Cref{thm: main.result} to the setting of measures whose support fill $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$

nodes.name: Continuity argument removing the hole assumption
nodes.statement_short: Apply Theorem 1.2 to orthant approximations from Lemma B.1 and use Lipschitz dependence on initial data; approximate targets similarly.

nodes.name: W-infinity stability of self-attention dynamics
nodes.statement:
Suppose $\mu_0,
u_0\in \mathscr{P}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})$, $ m{\mathit{B}}\in\mathscr{M}_{d	imes d}(\mathbb{R})$. Let $\mu$ and  $
u$ denote the unique solutions to \eqref{eq: cauchy.pb.W=0} on $\mathbb{R}_{\geqslant0}	imes\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ corresponding to data $\mu_0$ and $
u_0$ respectively. Then there exist a couple of constants $M_0\geqslant 1$ and $M_1>0$ depending only on $ m{\mathit{B}}$ such that 
     egin{equation*}
        \mathsf{W}_\infty(\mu(t),
u(t))\leqslant M_0e^{e^{M_1 t} }\,\mathsf{W}_\infty(\mu_0,
u_0)
    \end{equation*}
    for all $t\geqslant0$.
nodes.statement_short: $W_\infty(\mu(t),\nu(t)) \le M_0 e^{e^{M_1 t}} W_\infty(\mu_0,\nu_0)$ for the pure attention flow.
nodes.label: lem: gronwall.transfer.plan

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma C.1
nodes.statement_short: Push the optimal plan by the two flows, split by the triangle inequality and apply Gronwall twice, uniformly in p, then let $p\to\infty$.

nodes.name: Optimal plan and coupled flows
nodes.statement_short: Push the optimal plan through the product of the two flows.

nodes.name: Marginals of the pushed plan
nodes.statement_short: The pushed plan couples $\mu(t)$ and $\nu(t)$.

nodes.name: Triangle split
nodes.statement_short: Bound $W_p$ by two integrals.

nodes.name: Equation (C.1)
nodes.statement:
\mathsf{W}_p(\mu(t),\nu(t))&\leqslant \left(\iint d_g(\Phi^t(x),\Phi^t(y))^p\gamma_0(\, \mathrm{d} x,\, \mathrm{d} y)\right)^{\frac{1}{p}}\nonumber\\
        &+\left(\iint d_g(\Phi^t(y),\Psi^t(y))^p\gamma_0(\, \mathrm{d} x,\, \mathrm{d} y)\right)^{\frac{1}{p}}.
nodes.label: eq: gronwall.two.integrals

nodes.name: Gronwall for the first integral
nodes.statement_short: Lipschitz flow bound for the first integral.

nodes.name: Equation (C.2)
nodes.statement: \iint d_g(\Phi^t(x),\Phi^t(y))^p\gamma_0(\, \mathrm{d} x,\, \mathrm{d} y)&\leqslant K_1^pe^{pK_0 t} \iint d_g(x,y)^p\gamma_0(\, \mathrm{d} x,\, \mathrm{d} y)
nodes.label: eq: gronwall.fisrt

nodes.name: Gronwall for the second integral
nodes.statement_short: Differential inequality and Gronwall for the flow difference.

nodes.name: Equation (C.3)
nodes.statement: \iint d_g(\Phi^t(y),\Psi^t(y))^p\gamma_0(\, \mathrm{d} x,\, \mathrm{d} y)\leqslant C_2^p  \left(\int_0^t e^{C_1(t-s)}\mathsf{W}_p(\mu(s),\nu(s))\, \mathrm{d} s\right)^p.
nodes.label: eq: gronwall.second

nodes.name: Integral Gronwall and $p\to\infty$
nodes.statement_short: Integral Gronwall gives the double-exponential bound, uniform in p.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.2
nodes.statement_short: A variance Lyapunov functional around the normalized barycenter decays exponentially once the support is small; Markov's inequality gives $W_2$ decay and the barycenter direction converges exponentially.

nodes.name: Variance functional
nodes.statement:
Note that $\|\mathbb{E}_{\mu(t)}[x]\|>0$ since $\mathrm{supp}(\mu_0)$ is contained in a hemisphere.
Set 
$$
\gamma(t):=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\mu(t)}[x]}{\|\mathbb{E}_{\mu(t)}[x]\|}.
$$ 
and consider
\begin{equation*} 
    \mathsf{V}[\mu(t)](t):=\int\|x-\gamma(t)\|^2\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x).
\end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Define the normalized barycenter $\gamma(t)$ and the variance $\mathsf{V}$.

nodes.name: Exponential decay of the variance
nodes.statement_short: Show $\mathsf{V}$ decays exponentially.

nodes.name: Differentiate the variance
nodes.statement_short: Compute the time derivative of $\mathsf{V}$; supports are small after $t_0$.

nodes.name: Equation (C.4)
nodes.statement:
\frac{\, \mathrm{d}}{\, \mathrm{d} t} \mathsf{V}[\mu(t)](t)&=2\|\mathbb{E}_{\mu(t)}[x]\|\left(-1+\int \langle x, \gamma(t)\rangle^2\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)\right)\nonumber\\
     &\hspace{1cm}+2\int \langle x-\gamma(t),-\dot{\gamma}(t)\rangle \mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x).
nodes.label: eq: differentiation.lyapunov

nodes.name: Equation (C.5)
nodes.statement: d_g(x,y)\leqslant \varepsilon_0 \hspace{1cm} \text{ for all }x,y\in \mathrm{supp}(\mu(t_0)).
nodes.label: eq: smallness

nodes.name: First term
nodes.statement_short: Taylor expansion of the first term.

nodes.name: Equation (C.6)
nodes.statement:
-1+\int \langle x, \gamma(t)\rangle^2\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)&=-1+\int \cos^2\left(d_g(x,\gamma)\right)\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)\nonumber\\
     &=-1+\int\left(1-\frac{1}{2}d_g(x,\gamma)^2+O\left(\varepsilon_0^4\right)\right)^2\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)\nonumber\\
     &=-\int d_g(x,\gamma)^2\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)+O\left(\varepsilon_0^4\right).
nodes.label: eq: expectation.term

nodes.name: Derivative of $\gamma$
nodes.statement_short: Compute $\dot\gamma$ and plug into the second term.

nodes.name: Equation (C.7)
nodes.statement:
\dot{\gamma}(t)&=\int \bm{\mathsf{P}}^\perp_x(\gamma(t)) \mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)-\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\mu(t)}[x]}{\|\mathbb{E}_{\mu(t)}[x]\|^2}\left\langle \frac{\mathbb{E}_{\mu(t)}[x]}{\|\mathbb{E}_{\mu(t)}[x]\|},\int y\partial_t\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} y)\right\rangle\nonumber\\
     &=\int \bm{\mathsf{P}}^\perp_x(\gamma(t)) \mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)-\gamma(t)\left(1-\int \langle \gamma(t),x\rangle^2\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)\right).
nodes.label: eq: gamma.prime

nodes.name: Equation (C.8)
nodes.statement:
\int \langle y-\gamma(t),\dot{\gamma}(t)\rangle \mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} y)&=\int \langle y,\dot{\gamma}(t)\rangle \mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} y)-\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{\, \mathrm{d}}{\, \mathrm{d} t}\langle \gamma(t),\gamma(t)\rangle \mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} y) \nonumber\\
     &=\int \langle y,\dot{\gamma}(t)\rangle \mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} y).
nodes.label: eq: to.develop

nodes.name: Expand inner product
nodes.statement:
Expanding the inner product in \eqref{eq: to.develop}, we obtain
\begin{align}
    \langle y,\dot{\gamma}(t)\rangle&=\int\left\langle y,\bm{\mathsf{P}}^\perp_x\gamma(t)\right\rangle\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)-\left(1-\int \langle \gamma(t),x\rangle^2\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)\right) \langle y,\gamma(t)\rangle\nonumber\\
    &=\int\left(\langle y,\gamma(t)\rangle -\langle \gamma(t),x\rangle \langle x,y\rangle\right) \mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)
    \nonumber\\
    &\hspace{4cm}-\left(1-\int \langle \gamma(t),x\rangle^2\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)\right) \langle y,\gamma(t)\rangle\nonumber\\
    &=-\int \langle \gamma(t),x\rangle \langle x,y\rangle \mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)+\left(\int \langle \gamma(t),x\rangle^2\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)\right) \langle y,\gamma(t)\rangle\nonumber\\
    &=-\int  \cos(d_g(\gamma(t),x)) \cos(d_g(x,y)) \mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)\nonumber\\
    &\hspace{1.5cm}+\left(\int \cos^2(d_g(\gamma(t),x))\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)\right) \cos(d_g(y,\gamma(t))). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Express $\langle y,\dot\gamma\rangle$ with cosines of geodesic distances.

nodes.name: Equation (C.9)
nodes.statement:
\langle y,\dot{\gamma}(t)\rangle&=\int\left\langle y,\bm{\mathsf{P}}^\perp_x\gamma(t)\right\rangle\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)-\left(1-\int \langle \gamma(t),x\rangle^2\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)\right) \langle y,\gamma(t)\rangle\nonumber\\
    &=\int\left(\langle y,\gamma(t)\rangle -\langle \gamma(t),x\rangle \langle x,y\rangle\right) \mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)
    \nonumber\\
    &\hspace{4cm}-\left(1-\int \langle \gamma(t),x\rangle^2\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)\right) \langle y,\gamma(t)\rangle\nonumber\\
    &=-\int \langle \gamma(t),x\rangle \langle x,y\rangle \mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)+\left(\int \langle \gamma(t),x\rangle^2\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)\right) \langle y,\gamma(t)\rangle\nonumber\\
    &=-\int  \cos(d_g(\gamma(t),x)) \cos(d_g(x,y)) \mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)\nonumber\\
    &\hspace{1.5cm}+\left(\int \cos^2(d_g(\gamma(t),x))\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)\right) \cos(d_g(y,\gamma(t))).
nodes.label: eq: several.cosines

nodes.name: Taylor expansions
nodes.statement_short: Second-order expansions of the cosine terms.

nodes.name: Equation (C.10)
nodes.statement:
&\int  \cos(d_g(\gamma(t),x) )\cos(d_g(x,y)) \mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)\nonumber\\
    &=\int \left(1-\frac{d_g(\gamma(t),x)^2}{2}+O\left(\varepsilon_0^4\right)\right)\left(1-\frac{d_g(y,x)^2}{2}+O\left(\varepsilon_0^4\right)\right)\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)\nonumber\\
    &=\int \left(1-\frac{d_g(\gamma(t),x)^2}{2}-\frac{d_g(y,x)^2}{2}\right)\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)+O\left(\varepsilon_0^4\right),
nodes.label: eq: first.first.term

nodes.name: Equation (C.11)
nodes.statement:
&\left(\int \cos^2(d_g(\gamma(t),x))\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)\right) \cos(d_g(y,\gamma(t)))\nonumber\\
    &=\left(\int \left(1-d_g(\gamma(t),x)^2+O\left(\varepsilon_0^4\right)\right)\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)\right) \left(1-\frac{d_g(y,\gamma(t))^2}{2}+O\left(\varepsilon_0^4\right)\right)\nonumber\\
    &=\left(\int (1-d_g(\gamma(t),x)^2)\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)\right)-\frac{d_g(y,\gamma(t))^2}{2}+O\left(\varepsilon_0^4\right).
nodes.label: eq: first.second.term

nodes.name: Combine expansions
nodes.statement:
Combining \eqref{eq: first.first.term} and \eqref{eq: first.second.term} in \eqref{eq: several.cosines} we obtain
\begin{align*}
    \langle y,\dot{\gamma}(t)\rangle &=\left(\int (1-d_g(\gamma(t),x)^2)\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)\right)-\frac{d_g(y,\gamma(t))^2}{2}\nonumber\\
    &\hspace{0.5cm}-\int \left(1-\frac{d_g(\gamma(t),x)^2}{2}-\frac{d_g(y,x)^2}{2}\right)\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)+O\left(\varepsilon_0^4\right)\nonumber\\
    &=-\int d_g(\gamma(t),x)^2\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)-\frac{d_g(y,\gamma(t))^2}{2}\nonumber\\
    &\hspace{0.5cm}+\frac{1}{2}\int \left(d_g(\gamma(t),x)^2+d_g(y,x)^2\right)\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)+O\left(\varepsilon_0^4\right).
\end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Combine the expansions.

nodes.name: Assemble derivative
nodes.statement_short: Derivative of $\mathsf{V}$ is minus the pairwise spread up to $O(\varepsilon_0^3)$.

nodes.name: Equation (C.12)
nodes.statement:
\frac{\, \mathrm{d}}{\, \mathrm{d} t} \mathsf{V}[\mu(t)](t)&=2\|\mathbb{E}_{\mu(t)}[x]\|\left(-\int d_g(x,\gamma(t))^2\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)\right)-2\int \langle y,\dot{\gamma}(t)\rangle \mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} y)\nonumber\\
    &=-2\int d_g(x,\gamma(t))^2\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)+O\left(\varepsilon_0^3\right)\nonumber\\
    &\hspace{1cm} - \int d_g(\gamma(t),x)^2\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)-\iint d_g(y,x)^2\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} y)\nonumber\\
    &\hspace{1cm} +2\int d_g(\gamma(t),x)^2\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)+\int d_g(y,\gamma(t))^2\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} y),
nodes.label: eq: putting.together

nodes.name: Differential inequality
nodes.statement_short: Obtain a differential inequality and change variables.

nodes.name: Equation (C.13)
nodes.statement: \frac{\, \mathrm{d}}{\, \mathrm{d} t} \mathsf{V}[\mu(t)](t)\leqslant - c\iint \|y-x\|^2\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} y)
nodes.label: eq: diff.ineq.first

nodes.name: Equation (C.14)
nodes.statement: \frac{\, \mathrm{d}}{\, \mathrm{d} t} \mathsf{V}[\mu(t)](t)\leqslant - c\iint \|\gamma(t)+z-x\|^2\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)\nu(t,\, \mathrm{d} z)
nodes.label: eq: diff.ineq.first.reload

nodes.name: Gronwall
nodes.statement_short: Get $\dot{\mathsf{V}}\le -c_0\mathsf{V}$ and exponential decay by Gronwall.

nodes.name: Equation (C.15)
nodes.statement:
rac{\, \mathrm{d}}{\, \mathrm{d} t} \mathsf{V}[\mu(t)](t)&\leqslant - c\iint \left(\|\gamma(t)-x\|^2+\|z\|^2+2\langle z,\gamma(t)-xangleight)\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)
u(t,\, \mathrm{d} z)
onumber\
    &=- c\int\|\gamma(t)-x\|^2\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)-c\int \|z\|^2
u(\, \mathrm{d} z)
onumber\
    &\hspace{4cm}-2c\iint \langle z,\gamma(t)-xangle\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)
u(t,\, \mathrm{d} z)
onumber\
    &\leqslant -c\mathsf{V}[\mu(t)](t)+O\left(\varepsilon_0^3ight)
onumber\
    &\leqslant -c_0\mathsf{V}[\mu(t)](t)
nodes.label: eq: diff.ineq.second

nodes.name: Equation (C.16)
nodes.statement: \mathsf{V}[\mu(t)](t)\leqslant c_1e^{-c_0t}
nodes.label: eq: exp.decay

nodes.name: Split the W2 integral
nodes.statement:
We now use \eqref{eq: exp.decay} to conclude. We make use of  
\begin{align} \mathsf{W}_2^2\left(\mu(t),\updelta_{\gamma(t)}\right)&\lesssim\int \left\|x-\gamma(t)\right\|^2\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x) \\
&=\int_{\{\|x-\gamma(t)\|^2\leqslant\alpha\}} \left\|x-\gamma(t)\right\|^2\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)\nonumber\\
&\hspace{1cm}+\int_{\{\|x-\gamma(t)\|^2>\alpha\}} \left\|x-\gamma(t)\right\|^2\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x) \nonumber,
\end{align}
for $\alpha>0$ to be determined later on, where we recall the integrals are taken over $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$, and the first inequality follows by equivalence of norms and by considering the (optimal) transport plan which corresponds to $\mathsf{T}(x)=\gamma(t)$.
We only need to estimate the second term in \eqref{eq: W2.transport}.
nodes.statement_short: Bound $W_2^2$ by the variance split at level $\alpha$.

nodes.name: Equation (C.17)
nodes.statement:
\mathsf{W}_2^2\left(\mu(t),\updelta_{\gamma(t)}\right)&\lesssim\int \left\|x-\gamma(t)\right\|^2\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x) \\
&=\int_{\{\|x-\gamma(t)\|^2\leqslant\alpha\}} \left\|x-\gamma(t)\right\|^2\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)\nonumber\\
&\hspace{1cm}+\int_{\{\|x-\gamma(t)\|^2>\alpha\}} \left\|x-\gamma(t)\right\|^2\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x) \nonumber,
nodes.label: eq: W2.transport

nodes.name: Markov's inequality
nodes.statement_short: Markov's inequality gives exponential decay of $W_2$ to $\delta_{\gamma(t)}$.

nodes.name: Reduce to barycenter convergence
nodes.statement_short: It remains to show $\gamma(t)\to x_0$ exponentially.

nodes.name: Expand $\dot\gamma$
nodes.statement:
Similar computations to \eqref{eq: several.cosines} give
\begin{align*}
    \dot{\gamma}(t)&=\int \bm{\mathsf{P}}^\perp_x(\gamma(t))\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)-\gamma(t) \left(1-\int \langle \gamma(t),x\rangle^2\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)\right)\\
    &=-\int \cos(d_g(x,\gamma(t)))x\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)+\gamma(t)\int \cos^2(d_g(x,\gamma(t))\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)\\
    &=-\int \cos(d_g(x,\gamma(t)))x\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)+\gamma(t)\int \cos^2(d_g(x,\gamma(t))\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x).
\end{align*}
We Taylor expand in the above identity to find
\begin{align*}
    \dot{\gamma}(t)&=-\int\left(1-\frac{d_g(x,\gamma(t))^2}{2}\right)x\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)\nonumber\\
    &\hspace{3cm}+\gamma(t)\int (1-d_g(x,\gamma(t))^2)\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)+O\left(\varepsilon_0^4\right)\nonumber\\
    &=-\int\left(1-\frac{d_g(x,\gamma(t))^2}{2}\right)(x-\gamma(t)+\gamma(t))\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)\nonumber\\
    &\hspace{3cm}+\gamma(t)\int (1-d_g(x,\gamma(t))^2)\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)+O\left(\varepsilon_0^4\right)\nonumber\\
    &=-\int\left(1-\frac{d_g(x,\gamma(t))^2}{2}\right)(x-\gamma(t))\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)\nonumber\\
    &\hspace{4cm}-\frac{\gamma(t)}{2}\int d_g(x,\gamma(t))^2\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)+O\left(\varepsilon_0^4\right).
\end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Taylor expand $\dot\gamma$.

nodes.name: Bound $\dot\gamma$
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy-Schwarz gives $|\dot\gamma|\lesssim e^{-c_0t/2}$.

nodes.name: Equation (C.18)
nodes.statement:
&\left|\int\left(1-\frac{d_g(x,\gamma(t))^2}{2}\right)(x-\gamma(t))\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)\right|\nonumber\\
    &\hspace{1cm}\leqslant \left(\int\left(1-\frac{d_g(x,\gamma(t))^2}{2}\right)^2\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\left(\int\|x-\gamma(t)\|^2\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\nonumber\\
    &\hspace{1cm}\leqslant\sqrt{\mathsf{V}[\mu(t)](t)}\lesssim e^{-\frac{c_0}{2}t}.
nodes.label: eq: gam.dot.one

nodes.name: Equation (C.19)
nodes.statement: \left|\gamma(t)\int d_g(x,\gamma(t))^2\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)\right|\lesssim \int \|x-\gamma(t)\|^2\mu(t,\, \mathrm{d} x)\lesssim e^{-c_0t}.
nodes.label: eq: gam.dot.two

nodes.name: Integrate
nodes.statement_short: Integrating $\dot\gamma$ gives exponential convergence to $x_0$.

nodes.statement: \Phi^t(x)=x\hspace{1cm}\text{ for }x\notin \bigcup_{k=0}^K \mathscr{B}_k

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma C.3
nodes.section: C.3 Transporting mass through overlapping balls
nodes.statement_short: A ReLU field active only on the ball pulls its points monotonically towards a point of the overlap; the W1 estimate for the second part follows as in Prop. 2.3.

nodes.name: ReLU field active on the ball
nodes.section: C.3 Transporting mass through overlapping balls
nodes.statement_short: Choose a ReLU field active exactly on $\mathscr{B}_0$ pointing to $\omega$ in the overlap.

nodes.name: Field formula and monotonicity
nodes.section: C.3 Transporting mass through overlapping balls
nodes.statement_short: The field vanishes outside $\mathscr{B}_0$ and $\langle x,\omega\rangle$ increases inside.

nodes.name: Equation (C.23)
nodes.statement: \Big(-\cos d_g(z,x)+\cos(R)\Big)_+> 0\hspace{1cm}\iff \hspace{1cm} x\in\mathscr{B}_0.

nodes.name: Equation (C.24)

nodes.name: Mass reaches the overlap
nodes.statement:
We claim that this implies the existence of a time $T_\varepsilon>0$ for which
\begin{equation} \mu(T_\varepsilon,\mathscr{B}_0\cap\mathscr{B}_1)\geqslant(1-\varepsilon)\mu_0(\mathscr{B}_0).
\end{equation}
To prove this claim, let $\delta>0$ be fixed and to be determined later on. 
Because of \eqref{eq: dissipation.sphere}, there exists some $T_\delta>0$ such that
\begin{equation} \Phi^{T_\delta}(x)\in\mathscr{B}_0\cap\mathscr{B}_1\hspace{1cm}\text{ for }x\in B(z,R-\delta),
\end{equation}
where $\Phi^{T_\delta}:\mathbb{S}^{d-1}\to \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ is the flow map of \eqref{eq: neural.ode.sphere}. Since $\mu(T_\delta)=\Phi^{T_\delta}_\#\mu_0$, we have
\begin{equation} \mu(T_\delta, \mathscr{B}_0\cap\mathscr{B}_1)=\mu_0\Big((\Phi^{T_\delta})^{-1}(\mathscr{B}_0\cap\mathscr{B}_1)\Big)\overset{\eqref{eq: claim.lemmaA11}}{\geqslant}\mu_0(B(z,R-\delta)).
\end{equation}
Taking $\delta>0$ small enough so that $\mu_0(B(z,R-\delta))\geqslant (1-\varepsilon) \mu_0(\mathscr{B}_0)$ yields claim \eqref{eq: claim.lemmaA1}.

nodes.statement_short: Claim: by some time most mass of $\mathscr{B}_0$ lies in the overlap.

Because of \eqref{eq: dissipation.sphere}, there exists some $T_\delta>0$ such that
\begin{equation} \Phi^{T_\delta}(x)\in\mathscr{B}_0\cap\mathscr{B}_1\hspace{1cm}\text{ for }x\in B(z,R-\delta),
\end{equation}
where $\Phi^{T_\delta}:\mathbb{S}^{d-1}\to \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ is the flow map of \eqref{eq: neural.ode.sphere}.
nodes.section: C.3 Transporting mass through overlapping balls
nodes.statement_short: Points of a slightly shrunk ball enter the overlap in finite time.

nodes.name: Equation (C.26)
nodes.statement: \Phi^{T_\delta}(x)\in\mathscr{B}_0\cap\mathscr{B}_1\hspace{1cm}\text{ for }x\in B(z,R-\delta),
nodes.section: C.3 Transporting mass through overlapping balls
nodes.label: eq: claim.lemmaA11

nodes.name: Pushforward mass bound
nodes.section: C.3 Transporting mass through overlapping balls
nodes.statement_short: Pushforward gives the mass lower bound.

nodes.name: Equation (C.27)
nodes.statement: \mu(T_\delta, \mathscr{B}_0\cap\mathscr{B}_1)=\mu_0\Big((\Phi^{T_\delta})^{-1}(\mathscr{B}_0\cap\mathscr{B}_1)\Big)\overset{\eqref{eq: claim.lemmaA11}}{\geqslant}\mu_0(B(z,R-\delta)).
nodes.section: C.3 Transporting mass through overlapping balls
nodes.label: eq: mass.concentration

nodes.name: Choose $\delta$
nodes.statement: Taking $\delta>0$ small enough so that $\mu_0(B(z,R-\delta))\geqslant (1-\varepsilon) \mu_0(\mathscr{B}_0)$ yields claim \eqref{eq: claim.lemmaA1}.
nodes.section: C.3 Transporting mass through overlapping balls
nodes.statement_short: Choosing $\delta$ small proves the claim.

nodes.name: First part
nodes.statement:
We conclude that \eqref{eq: claim.statement.lemmaA1} holds by rescaling time. Finally, by virtue of \eqref{eq: activation.ball}, the flow map $\Phi^t$ is such that $\Phi^t(x)=x$ for
$x\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}\setminus\mathscr{B}_0$ and $t\in[0,T]$.
nodes.section: C.3 Transporting mass through overlapping balls
nodes.statement_short: Rescale time; the flow fixes the complement of $\mathscr{B}_0$.

nodes.name: Second part via duality
nodes.section: C.3 Transporting mass through overlapping balls
nodes.statement_short: Take $\mathscr{B}_1$ a small ball around $\omega$ and argue as in Prop. 2.3.

nodes.name: Bound inside $\mathscr{B}_0$
nodes.statement:
Let $\overline{\varepsilon}>0$ be arbitrary and to be chosen small enough later.
Using \eqref{eq: mass.concentration}---with $\overline{\varepsilon}$ instead of $\varepsilon$---and the definition of $\mathscr{B}_1$, we find  
\begin{align*}
    \left|\int_{\mathscr{B}_0\setminus\mathscr{B}_1} \phi \left(\mu(T_\delta) -\alpha\right)+ \int_{\mathscr{B}_1} \phi \left(\mu(T_\delta) -\alpha\right)\right|&\leqslant \left|\int_{\mathscr{B}_0\setminus\mathscr{B}_1} \phi \left(\mu(T_\delta) -\alpha\right)\right|\\
      &\hspace{-6cm}+ \left|\int_{\mathscr{B}_1} \phi \mu(T_\delta) -  \mu(T_\delta,\mathscr{B}_1)\phi(\omega)-(\mu_0(\mathscr{B}_0)-\mu(T_\delta,\mathscr{B}_1))\phi(\omega)\right|\\ &\hspace{-6cm}\leqslant\|\nabla\phi\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})}\cdot\eta\cdot\overline{\varepsilon}\cdot\mu_0(\mathscr{B}_0)+\eta+\overline{\varepsilon}\cdot\mu_0(\mathscr{B}_0),
\end{align*}
which tends to $0$ as $\overline{\varepsilon}$ and $\eta$ tend to zero.
nodes.section: C.3 Transporting mass through overlapping balls
nodes.statement_short: The contribution inside $\mathscr{B}_0$ is small.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.section: C.3 Transporting mass through overlapping balls
nodes.statement_short: Nothing changes outside; choose parameters small.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma C.2
nodes.section: C.3 Transporting mass through overlapping balls
nodes.statement_short: Backward induction along the chain, applying Lemma C.3 on each consecutive pair of balls.

nodes.name: Backward induction
nodes.section: C.3 Transporting mass through overlapping balls
nodes.statement_short: Split time and apply Lemma C.3 on the last pair of balls.

nodes.name: Unroll the induction
nodes.section: C.3 Transporting mass through overlapping balls
nodes.statement_short: Disjointness of non-consecutive balls yields the product bound.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.3
nodes.statement_short: Use attention along an orthonormal basis orthogonal to the chosen barycenter to expel the other measures from the orthant, cluster the chosen measures with a perceptron, then reverse the first flow.

nodes.name: Induction setup
nodes.statement_short: WLOG j=N; induct on N assuming the first N-1 supports disjoint.

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement_short: Goal: a solution map separating the N-th measure and $\nu_0$ from the others.

nodes.name: Expel the other measures
nodes.statement_short: Attention along a basis orthogonal to the N-th barycenter expels the other measures from the orthant.

nodes.name: Attention along a basis
nodes.statement:
Throughout this first step, $\bm{\mathit{W}}\equiv0$.
Consider $0<T_0<T_1<\ldots<T_{d-1}$ to be chosen later on, and set
\begin{equation*}
    \bm{\mathit{V}}(t)=\sum_{k=1}^{d-1}\alpha_k\alpha_k^\top 1_{[T_{k-1},T_k]}(t)
\end{equation*}
with $\{\alpha_k\}_{k\in[d-1]}$ being an orthonormal basis of $\mathrm{span }\left(\left\{\mathbb{E}_{\mu_0^N}[z]\right\}\right)^\perp$, namely 
$$\left \langle \mathbb{E}_{\mu_0^N}[x],\alpha_k\right\rangle=0$$ 
for all $k\in[d-1]$.
nodes.statement_short: Set $V$ to successive rank-one projections on an orthonormal basis orthogonal to the barycenter.

nodes.name: Barycenter evolution
nodes.statement_short: The barycenter component along $\alpha_1$ evolves exponentially without sign change.

nodes.name: Equation (C.28)
nodes.label: eq: cauchy.pb.reloaded

nodes.name: Points converge to $\pm\alpha_1$
nodes.statement_short: Measures with nonzero component cluster near $\pm\alpha_1$.

nodes.name: Repeat for all k
nodes.statement:
We can repeat the argument for every $k$ to deduce
\begin{equation} \mathrm{supp}(\mu(T_{d-1}))\subset \bigcup_{k\in[d-1]} B(\alpha_k,C_{k}\varepsilon_k)\cup B(-\alpha_k,C_{k}\varepsilon_k)
\end{equation}
where $C_k>0$  does not depend on $\varepsilon_k$, but does depend on  $\varepsilon_\ell$ for $\ell>k$. 
We can choose all radii $\varepsilon_k$ small enough so that
    \begin{equation} \bigcup_{k\in[d-1]} B(\alpha_k,C_{k}\varepsilon_k)\cup B(-\alpha_k,C_{k}\varepsilon_k)\subset\mathbb{S}^{d-1}\setminus\mathbb{Q}_1^{d-1}.
    \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Repeating gives supports in small balls outside the orthant.

nodes.name: Equation (C.29)
nodes.statement: \mathrm{supp}(\mu(T_{d-1}))\subset \bigcup_{k\in[d-1]} B(\alpha_k,C_{k}\varepsilon_k)\cup B(-\alpha_k,C_{k}\varepsilon_k)
nodes.label: eq: supports.in.balls

nodes.name: Equation (C.30)
nodes.statement: \bigcup_{k\in[d-1]} B(\alpha_k,C_{k}\varepsilon_k)\cup B(-\alpha_k,C_{k}\varepsilon_k)\subset\mathbb{S}^{d-1}\setminus\mathbb{Q}_1^{d-1}.
nodes.label: eq: union.out

nodes.name: Map $\Psi_1$
nodes.statement:
Whence we have constructed a map 
$$\Psi_{1}:\mathscr{P}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})\to\mathscr{P}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1}),$$
with $\Psi_1(\mu_0)=\mu(T_d)$ where $\mu$ denotes the solution to the Cauchy problem \eqref{eq: cauchy.pb.reloaded} with the choice of parameters specified at the very beginning.  Since $\mathbb{E}_{\mu_0^i}[x]$ is not colinear with $\mathbb{E}_{\mu_0^N}[x]$, and thanks to \eqref{eq: supports.in.balls} and \eqref{eq: union.out},
$$\mathrm{supp}\,\Psi_1(\mu^j_0)\subset\mathbb{S}^{d-1}\setminus\mathbb{Q}_1^{d-1}$$ for $j\in[N-1]$, and 
$$\Psi_1(\mu^N_0)=\mu^N_0,\hspace{1cm} \Psi_1(\nu_0)=\nu_0.$$
nodes.statement_short: $\Psi_1$ expels the other measures and fixes $\mu_0^N,\nu_0$.

nodes.name: Cluster the chosen measures
nodes.statement_short: A perceptron field active only on the orthant clusters $\mu^N$ and $\nu$ near the barycenter direction.

nodes.name: Separating half-space
nodes.statement_short: Choose a half-space containing the orthant but not the expelled measures.

nodes.name: Perceptron parameters
nodes.statement_short: Set the perceptron towards the barycenter direction.

nodes.name: Clustering near the barycenter
nodes.statement_short: Other measures are invariant; the chosen ones enter a $\delta$-ball.

nodes.name: Equation (C.31)
nodes.statement: \mathrm{supp}\left(\nu(T_\delta)\right)\cup\mathrm{supp}\left(\mu^N(T_\delta)\right)\subset B\left(  \frac{\mathbb{E}_{\mu_0^N}[x]}{\|\mathbb{E}_{\mu_0^N}[x]\|},\delta\right).
nodes.label: eq: inclusion

nodes.name: Map $\Psi_2$
nodes.statement:
This construction yields a flow map 
$$\Psi_2:\mathscr{P}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})\to\mathscr{P}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1}),$$ 
with 
$$\Psi_2(\mu_0)=\mu(T_\delta)$$
where $\mu$ denotes the solution to the Cauchy problem \eqref{eq: cauchy.pb} on $[T_d, T_\delta]$ with the choice of parameters specified in this step, which satisfies 
$$\Psi_2(\mu^j(T_d))=\mu^j(T_d)$$ for $j\in[N-1]$,
and $\Psi_2(\mu^N(T_d)),\Psi_2(\nu(T_d))$
satisfy \eqref{eq: inclusion}.
nodes.statement_short: Define $\Psi_2$.

nodes.name: Reverse the first flow
nodes.statement_short: Apply $\Psi_1^{-1}$ and choose $\delta$ small.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.4
nodes.statement_short: Part 1: move mass of a discriminating ball to a well-chosen point. Part 2: a short attention phase makes supports differ, then the Part 1 construction breaks colinearity.

nodes.name: First part
nodes.statement: We begin with the first part of the statement. As before, we can take all time horizons to be as large as desired throughout by rescaling the norm of the parameters.
nodes.statement_short: Start with part 1; horizons can be enlarged by rescaling.

nodes.name: Part 1
nodes.statement_short: Move the mass of a discriminating ball to a well-chosen point.

nodes.name: Discriminating ball
nodes.statement_short: Take a ball with different masses under the two measures.

nodes.name: Choice of $x^*$
nodes.statement_short: Some $x^*$ in the ball makes the modified barycenters differ, else contradiction.

nodes.name: Parameters
nodes.statement:
Let $a\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ be the center of $\mathscr{B}$ and $R>0$ its radius. 
Consider
\begin{align} \bm{\mathit{U}} &= -{\bf1}a^\top,\\ 
b&= R {\bf1}, \nonumber
\end{align}
and any $\bm{\mathit{W}}\in\mathscr{M}_{d\times d}(\mathbb{R})$ satisfying
\begin{equation} \bm{\mathit{W}} {\bf1}=x^*.
\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Choose a ReLU field active on the ball pointing to $x^*$.

nodes.name: Equation (C.32)
nodes.statement:
\bm{\mathit{U}} &= -{\bf1}a^\top,\\ 
b&= R {\bf1}, \nonumber
nodes.label: eq: controls.1

nodes.name: Equation (C.33)
nodes.statement: \bm{\mathit{W}} {\bf1}=x^*.
nodes.label: eq: controls.2

nodes.name: Apply Lemma C.3
nodes.statement_short: Lemma C.3 concentrates the ball mass at $x^*$.

nodes.name: Barycenters differ
nodes.statement:
Since the expectation of a measure is continuous with respect to the measure in the sense of the Wasserstein distance, it follows that there is a Lipschitz invertible flow map $\Phi:\mathbb{S}^{d-1}	o\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ of \eqref{eq: neural.ode.sphere} such that $\mathbb{E}_{\Phi_\#\mu_0}[x]
eq\mathbb{E}_{\Phi_\#
u_0}[x]$. Furthermore, $\Phi(x)=x$ for $x
otin\mathscr{B}$ by construction.
nodes.statement_short: Continuity of expectations gives different barycenters.

nodes.name: Part 2
nodes.statement_short: Attention first, then the Part 1 construction.

nodes.name: Parameter form
nodes.statement:
The parameters take the form
\begin{align*}
\bm{\mathit{V}}(t)&= I_d 1_{[0,T_*]}(t) & 
\bm{\mathit{W}}(t)&= \bm{\mathit{W}} 1_{[T_*,T]}(t) \\
\bm{\mathit{U}}(t)&= \bm{\mathit{U}} 1_{[T_*,T]}(t) &
b(t)&=b 1_{[T_*,T]}(t),
\end{align*}
for $T_*>0$ and $T>T_*$ to be determined later on. Recall that $\bm{\mathit{B}}\equiv0$.
nodes.statement_short: Attention on $[0,T_*]$ then perceptron on $[T_*,T]$.

nodes.name: Supports become different
nodes.statement_short: If supports coincide, a short attention phase makes them differ.

nodes.name: Equation (C.34)
nodes.statement: \mathrm{supp}(\mu_0)\neq\mathrm{supp}(\nu_0)
nodes.label: eq: diff.support

nodes.name: Strict separation estimate
nodes.statement_short: Boundary points of $\nu$ move further inward than those of $\mu$.

nodes.name: Discriminating ball
nodes.statement_short: Obtain a ball meeting $\nu(T_*)$ but not $\mu(T_*)$.

nodes.name: Equation (C.35)
nodes.statement: \mathscr{B}\cap\mathrm{supp}(\nu(T_*))\neq \varnothing,\quad \mathscr{B}\cap \mathrm{supp}(\mu(T_*))=\varnothing
nodes.label: eq: discriminatory.ball

nodes.name: Perceptron phase
nodes.statement:
Let $a\in \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ be the center of $\mathscr{B}$ and $R$ be its radius. Now, in the interval $(T_*,T)$ we take $\bm{\mathit{V}}\equiv0$ and $\bm{\mathit{W}},\bm{\mathit{U}}\in \mathscr{M}_{d\times d}(\mathbb{R})$ and $b\in \mathbb{R}^d$ as in \eqref{eq: controls.1}--\eqref{eq: controls.2}
    
    
    
    for some $x^*\in \mathscr{B}$ to be determined later on.  Because of \eqref{eq: discriminatory.ball}, $\nu$ is invariant with respect to the flow generated by the parameters defined in \eqref{eq: controls.1} and \eqref{eq: controls.2}.
nodes.statement_short: Use the Part 1 parameters; $\nu$ is invariant.

nodes.name: Break colinearity
nodes.statement_short: Choose $x^*$ so the barycenters are not colinear.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.1
nodes.statement_short: Define $\Psi^i = T^i_{\Phi_3}\circ T^i\circ (T^i_{\Phi_1})^{-1}$ and glue them on the disjoint supports.

nodes.name: Flows as maps
nodes.statement_short: The disentangling flows act by Lipschitz invertible maps.

nodes.name: Disjoint images
nodes.statement_short: The pushed supports are pairwise disjoint.

nodes.name: Equation (C.36)
nodes.statement: \mathrm{supp}\left(\left(\mathsf{T}^i_{\Phi_1}\right)_\#\mu_0^i\right)\cap \mathrm{supp}\left(\left(\mathsf{T}^j_{\Phi_1}\right)_\#\mu_0^j\right)=\varnothing,
nodes.label: eq: separated

nodes.name: Define $\Psi^i$
nodes.statement_short: Solve for $\Psi^i$ by conjugating $\mathsf{T}^i$.

nodes.name: Glue
nodes.statement: Due to \eqref{eq: separated}, there also exists a Lipschitz-continuous map $\Psi:\mathbb{S}^{d-1}\to \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ satisfying \eqref{eq: diffeo.supports}.
nodes.statement_short: Glue the $\Psi^i$ on disjoint supports.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.4
nodes.statement_short: Approximate the map by a simple function, split the measure into finitely many atoms plus a diffuse part, match atoms exactly and cluster diffuse pieces then match them.

nodes.name: Simple-function approximation
nodes.statement_short: Approximate $\Psi$ by a simple function and $\mu$ by $\mu^\eta$.

nodes.name: Equation (C.37)
nodes.statement: \Psi^\dagger_\varepsilon(x):=\sum_{m=1}^{M(\varepsilon)} y_m^\varepsilon 1_{\Omega_m(\varepsilon)}(x),
nodes.label: eq: simple.function

nodes.name: Equation (C.38)
nodes.statement: \bigcup_{m\in[M(\varepsilon)]} \Omega_m(\varepsilon) = \mathbb{S}^{d-1},
nodes.label: eq: partition

nodes.name: Equation (C.39)
nodes.statement: \left\|\Psi^\dagger_\varepsilon-\Psi\right\|_{L^2(\mu)}\leqslant \frac{\varepsilon}{2}.
nodes.label: eq: approx.by.simple.function

nodes.name: Equation (C.40)
nodes.statement:
\int \left\|\Psi_\varepsilon(x)-\sum_{m=1}^{M(\varepsilon)}y_m^\varepsilon 1_{\Omega_m}\right\|^2\mu(\, \mathrm{d} x)&=\int \left\|\Psi_\varepsilon(x)-\sum_{m=1}^{M(\varepsilon)}y_m^\varepsilon 1_{\Omega_m}\right\|^2\mu^\eta(\, \mathrm{d} x)\nonumber\\
    &+\int\left\|\Psi_\varepsilon(x)-\Psi^\dagger_\varepsilon(x)\right\|^2(\mu(\, \mathrm{d} x)-\mu^\eta(\, \mathrm{d} x))\nonumber\\
    &\hspace{-0.5cm}\leqslant \int \left\|\Psi_\varepsilon(x)-\sum_{m=1}^{M(\varepsilon)}y_m^\varepsilon 1_{\Omega_m}\right\|^2\mu^\eta(\, \mathrm{d} x)+2\pi\eta.
nodes.label: eq: TV.implication

nodes.name: Construct $\mu^\eta$
nodes.statement_short: Keep finitely many atoms and remove diffuse mass near them.

nodes.name: Lebesgue decomposition
nodes.statement_short: Split into atomic and diffuse parts and truncate atoms.

nodes.name: Remove diffuse mass near atoms
nodes.statement_short: Remove diffuse mass in small balls around atoms.

nodes.name: Equation (C.41)
nodes.statement: B(x_n,\eta_1)\cap B(x_m,\eta_1)=\varnothing \hspace{1cm} \text{ for } m\neq n\in[N(\eta)].
nodes.label: eq: balls.small

nodes.name: Equation (C.42)
nodes.statement: \mu^\eta:=\mu_{\text{pp}}^\eta+\mu_{\text{diff}}^\eta,
nodes.label: eq: Lebesgue.decomp

nodes.name: Equation (C.43)
nodes.statement: \mu_{\text{diff}}^{\eta}(A):=\mu_{\text{diff}}\left(A\setminus \bigcup_{n\in[N(\eta)]} B(x_n,\eta_1)\right)
nodes.label: eq: removing.mass.from.mu

nodes.name: Reduction to a matching problem
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to matching diffuse pieces to atoms and atoms exactly.

nodes.name: Pieces $\mu_m$
nodes.statement:
We further decompose $\mu^\eta$ in several parts. For $m\in[M(\varepsilon)]$, consider 
\begin{equation} \mu_m(A):=\mu^\eta_{\text{diff}}(A\cap\Omega_m)
\end{equation}
for any Borel $A\subset \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Restrict the diffuse part to each $\Omega_m$.

nodes.name: Equation (C.44)
nodes.statement: \mu_m(A):=\mu^\eta_{\text{diff}}(A\cap\Omega_m)
nodes.label: eq: mu.m

nodes.name: Split the error
nodes.statement_short: The error splits into diffuse and atomic contributions.

nodes.name: Equation (C.45)
nodes.statement: \mu^\eta_{\mathrm{diff}}(A) = \sum_{m=1}^{M(\varepsilon)} \mu_m(A)
nodes.label: eq: mu.eta.mu.m

nodes.name: Equation (C.46)
nodes.statement:
&\int \left\|\Psi_\varepsilon(x)-\sum_{m=1}^{M(\varepsilon)}y_m^\varepsilon 1_{\Omega_m}\right\|^2\mu^\eta(\, \mathrm{d} x)\nonumber\\
    &=\sum_{m=1}^{M(\varepsilon)}\int\left\|\Psi_\varepsilon(x)-y_m^\varepsilon\right\|^2\mu_m+\sum_{n=1}^{N(\eta)}\mu(\{x_n\})\left\|\Psi_\varepsilon(x_n)-\Psi^\dagger_\varepsilon(x_n)\right\|^2.
nodes.label: eq: new.bound

nodes.name: Trivial split
nodes.statement_short: Split each diffuse term over a small ball.

nodes.name: Equation (C.47)
nodes.statement:
&\int\left\|\Psi_\varepsilon(x)-y_m^\varepsilon\right\|^2\mu_m(\, \mathrm{d} x)\nonumber\\
    &=\mu_m(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})\Bigg(\int_{(\Psi_\varepsilon)^{-1}(B(x_m,\eta_3))} \|\Psi_\varepsilon(x)-y_m^\varepsilon\|^2\frac{\mu_m(\, \mathrm{d} x)}{\mu_m(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})}\nonumber\\&\hspace{2cm}+\int_{(\Psi_\varepsilon)^{-1}(B(x_m,\eta_3))^c} \|\Psi_\varepsilon(x)-y_m^\varepsilon\|^2\frac{\mu_m(\, \mathrm{d} x)}{\mu_m(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})}\Bigg) .
nodes.label: eq: trivial.split

nodes.name: Claim 2
nodes.statement_short: State and prove Claim 2.

nodes.name: Claim 2: W2-closeness to a Dirac gives mass in a ball
nodes.statement_short: If $W_2(\mu,\delta_{x_0})\le\eta_2$ then the mass outside $B(x_0,\eta_3)$ is $O(\eta_2/\eta_3)$.
nodes.label: cl: W.to.ball

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 2
nodes.statement_short: Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality tested against a Lipschitz cutoff function.

nodes.name: Apply Claim 2
nodes.statement_short: Claim 2 bounds each diffuse term.

nodes.name: Equation (C.48)
nodes.statement: \int\left\|\Psi_\varepsilon(x)-y_m\right\|^2\mu_m(\, \mathrm{d} x)\leqslant\mu_m(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})\left(\eta_3^2+2\pi\cdot  C\cdot \frac{\eta_2}{\eta_3}\right).
nodes.label: eq: estimate.in.m

nodes.name: Matching problem
nodes.statement_short: State the sufficient matching problem.

nodes.name: Construct the flow
nodes.statement_short: Compose exact atom matching, clustering and atom matching.

nodes.name: Composition
nodes.statement:
We look to use \Cref{prop: compression} to cluster the diffuse input measures to a single atom, which paired with \Cref{prop: targets.atoms} for matching all atoms approximately, would lead to the desired conclusion. 
Specifically, we construct the approximation candidate $\Psi_\varepsilon:\mathbb{S}^{d-1}\to\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ as
\begin{equation} \Psi_\varepsilon:=\Phi_3\circ \Phi_2\circ \Phi_1,
\end{equation}
where
nodes.statement_short: Define $\Psi_\varepsilon$ as a composition of three flows.

nodes.name: Equation (C.49)
nodes.statement: \Psi_\varepsilon:=\Phi_3\circ \Phi_2\circ \Phi_1,
nodes.label: eq: final.flow

nodes.name: $\Phi_1$
nodes.statement: $\Phi_1:\mathbb{S}^{d-1}\to \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ is the flow map induced by \Cref{prop: interpolation.neural.ode}\footnote{Should the assumption in \Cref{prop: interpolation.neural.ode} not hold, one can always choose slightly different \(y_m^\varepsilon\) in \eqref{eq: simple.function} so that the approximation error is not altered and the assumption does hold.}, which exactly matches $\mu(\{x_n\})\updelta_{x_n}$ to $\mu(\{x_n\})\updelta_{\Psi^\dagger_\varepsilon(x_n)}$, for all $n\in[N(\eta)]$;
nodes.statement_short: Exact atom matching by Prop. 4.1.

nodes.name: $\Phi_2$
nodes.statement: $\Phi_2:\mathbb{S}^{d-1}\to \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ is the flow map induced by \Cref{prop: compression} that concentrates $\mu_m$ near some atom inside $\mathrm{supp}(\Phi_{1\#}\mu_m)$, for all $m\in[M(\varepsilon)]$;
nodes.statement_short: Clustering by Prop. 2.3.

nodes.name: $\Phi_3$
nodes.statement: $\Phi_3:\mathbb{S}^{d-1}\to \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ is the flow map induced by \Cref{prop: interpolation.neural.ode} that matches the atoms from the previous step to $\mu_m(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})\updelta_{y_m^\varepsilon}$, for all $m\in[M(\varepsilon)]$.
nodes.statement_short: Matching cluster atoms by Prop. 4.1.

nodes.name: Make precise
nodes.statement: We now make the construction of \eqref{eq: final.flow} precise, and with the help of \eqref{eq: estimate.in.m}, \Cref{prop: compression}, and \Cref{prop: interpolation.neural.ode}, we bound the right hand side in \eqref{eq: new.bound}.
nodes.statement_short: Make the construction precise and bound the error.

nodes.name: Atoms matched exactly
nodes.statement_short: Exact matching of atoms.

nodes.name: Equation (C.50)
nodes.statement: \sum_{n=1}^{N(\eta)} \mu(\{x_n\})\left\|\Phi_1(x_n)-\Psi^\dagger_\varepsilon(x_n)\right\|^2=0.
nodes.label: eq: first.flow.discrete

nodes.name: Cluster diffuse pieces
nodes.statement_short: Clustering leaves atoms fixed.

nodes.name: Equation (C.51)
nodes.statement: \Phi_2\bigg|_{\left(\mathbb{S}^{d-1}\setminus\bigcup_{m\in[M(\varepsilon)]} \mathrm{supp}(\Phi_{1\#}\mu_m)\right)}\equiv\mathrm{Id}.
nodes.label: eq: identity.flow.2

nodes.name: Match cluster atoms
nodes.statement_short: Matching the cluster atoms keeps the atomic part exact.

nodes.name: Equation (C.52)
nodes.statement: \mathsf{W}_2\left(\Big(\Phi_3\circ\Phi_2\circ\Phi_1\Big)_{\#}\frac{\mu_m}{\mu_m(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})}  ,\updelta_{y_m^\varepsilon}\right)\leqslant C_{M(\varepsilon)}\cdot \eta_2
nodes.label: eq: close.in.W2

nodes.name: Combine estimates
nodes.statement_short: Combine the estimates.

nodes.name: Diffuse error small
nodes.statement_short: The diffuse error is at most $\varepsilon_1$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement_short: Conclude with the simple-function approximation.

nodes.name: Number of switches in the approximation lemma
Squashing to the equator
nodes.statement_short: A perceptron flow with $2(d-2)$ switches collapses each measure close to its 2D marginal on a great circle.
conclusions: Moreover, we can take $\bm{\mathit{B}}\equiv\bm{\mathit{V}}\equiv b\equiv0$, and $\bm{\mathit{W}}$ and $\bm{\mathit{U}}$ piecewise constant with at most $2(d-2)$ switches.
nodes.label: lem: squashing.lemma

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma D.1
nodes.statement_short: Collapse one coordinate at a time to the equator with two opposite ReLU fields, and combine by continuity estimates.

nodes.name: Induction on coordinates
nodes.statement: The proof is done by induction---it is thus enough to prove that we can ``collapse'' one dimension/coordinate. We begin by the last coordinate.
nodes.statement_short: Collapse one coordinate at a time.

nodes.name: Partial marginals
nodes.statement_short: Define partial marginals $\nu_k^i$.

nodes.name: Squashing field
nodes.statement_short: A ReLU field pushes the upper hemisphere to the equator.

nodes.name: Equation (D.1)
nodes.label: eq: squashing.upper.hemisphere

nodes.name: Combine both hemispheres
nodes.statement_short: Compose the two hemisphere flows.

nodes.name: First coordinate collapsed
nodes.statement_short: Choose $T_d$ to approximate the marginal.

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement_short: Assume the claim for later coordinates and collapse one more.

nodes.name: Equation (D.2)
nodes.statement: \mathsf{W}_2\left(\left(\Psi_4^{T_4}\circ\cdots\circ \Psi_d^{T_d}\right)_{\#}\mu_0^i,\nu^i_{3}\otimes\updelta^{\otimes(d-3)}_0\right)\leqslant\varepsilon_{4}
nodes.label: eq: heredity

nodes.name: Equation (D.3)
nodes.statement: \mathsf{W}_2\left(\left(\Psi_3^{T_3}\right)_\# \nu_{3}^i, \nu^i\otimes\updelta_0^{\otimes(d-3)}\right)\leqslant\varepsilon_3.
nodes.label: eq: epsilon.3

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement:
Then using standard continuity estimates for the continuity equation, along with \eqref{eq: epsilon.3}, \eqref{eq: heredity} and the triangle inequality, we deduce
\begin{align*}
&\mathsf{W}_2\left(\left(\Psi_3^{T_3}\circ\Psi_4^{T_4}\circ\cdots\circ \Psi_d^{T_d}\right)_{\#}\mu_0^i,\nu^i\otimes\updelta^{\otimes(d-3)}_0\right)\\
&\hspace{2cm}\leqslant\mathsf{W}_2\left(\left(\Psi_3^{T_3}\circ \Psi_4^{T_4}\circ\cdots\circ\Psi_d^{T_d}\right)_{\#}\mu_0^i, \left(\Psi_3^{T_3}\right)_\# \nu_{3}^i\right) \\
&\hspace{4cm} + \mathsf{W}_2\left(\left(\Psi_3^{T_3}\right)_\# \nu_{3}^i, \nu^i\otimes\updelta_0^{\otimes(d-2)} \right)\\
&\hspace{2cm}\leqslant C({\varepsilon_3}) \varepsilon_4 + \varepsilon_3
\end{align*}
    for some $C({\varepsilon_3})>0$. We may choose $\varepsilon_4$ and $\varepsilon_3$ small enough to conclude.
nodes.statement_short: Continuity estimates and the triangle inequality conclude.

nodes.name: Disentangling through continuous feedback
nodes.statement_short: With attention matrix B in continuous feedback form, measures whose circle marginals have disjoint support boundaries can be disentangled.
conclusions: Then there exists $\theta\in L^\infty((0,T);\Uptheta)$ such that
nodes.label: lem: feedback

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition D.2
nodes.statement_short: Squash to the circle, create an atom at the top point, keep it fixed by a feedback perceptron so attention clusters that measure near it, separate it and rotate it away; induct.

nodes.name: Setup
nodes.statement: We proceed in several steps. Throughout, $\bm{\mathit{V}}\equiv I_d$ and $b\equiv0$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix $V=I_d$ and $b=0$.

nodes.name: Reduce to the circle quadrant
nodes.statement_short: Lemmas D.1 and 3.2 reduce to measures on the quarter circle.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma D.1
nodes.statement:
By virtue of \Cref{lem: squashing.lemma}, for any $\varepsilon>0$ we can find a flow map $\Phi_{\varepsilon}:\mathbb{S}^{d-1}\to\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ induced by the characteristics of \eqref{eq: cauchy.pb} such that 
\begin{equation} \mathsf{W}_2\left(\Phi_{\varepsilon\#}\mu_0^i, \eta_0^i\otimes\updelta_0^{\otimes(d-2)}\right)\leqslant\varepsilon,
\end{equation}
where $\eta^i_0=\Psi_\#\nu_0^i\in\mathscr{P}(\mathbb{S}^1\cap(\mathbb{R}_{\geqslant0})^2)$, with $\Psi$ being the flow map given by \Cref{lem: first.quadrant}.
nodes.statement_short: Squash and transport to the first quadrant.

nodes.name: Equation (D.4)
nodes.statement: \mathsf{W}_2\left(\Phi_{\varepsilon\#}\mu_0^i, \eta_0^i\otimes\updelta_0^{\otimes(d-2)}\right)\leqslant\varepsilon,
nodes.label: eq: almost.first.quadrant

nodes.name: WLOG on $\mathbb{Q}_1^1$
nodes.statement: Since $\varepsilon>0$ can be chosen arbitrarily small, by virtue of \eqref{eq: almost.first.quadrant} we can,  without loss of generality, assume that $\mu_0^i$ are defined on $\mathbb{Q}_1^1:=\mathbb{S}^1\cap(\mathbb{R}_{\geqslant0})^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume the measures live on the quarter circle.

nodes.name: Atom at the top point
nodes.statement_short: Lemma C.3 creates an atom at the highest point of the first measure.

nodes.name: Order by top point
nodes.statement:
We order (and relabel) the measures $\mu^i_0$ by decreasing order of the respective magnitude of 
$$x^{i+}:=\mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}\limits_{x\in\mathrm{supp}(\mu^i_0)}\langle x, e_2\rangle.$$
Let $\eta>0$ be chosen later on.
nodes.statement_short: Order measures by their highest point.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma C.3
nodes.statement_short: Collapse a small ball around $x^{1+}$ to an atom.

nodes.name: Equation (D.5)
nodes.statement: \mathsf{W}_2\left(\mu^1(T_1(\eta)),\alpha\right)\leqslant\delta,
nodes.label: eq: atom.in.argmax

nodes.name: Others unchanged
nodes.statement_short: Other measures are unaffected.

nodes.name: Feedback perceptron
nodes.statement_short: A feedback perceptron keeps the atom fixed so attention clusters the first measure near it.

nodes.name: Perceptron only on the first measure
nodes.statement:
Let $T_2(\eta)>T_1(\eta)$ be chosen later on.
For $t\in[T_1(\eta), T_2(\eta)]$ we choose 
$$\bm{\mathit{U}}(t)\equiv {\bf1}^\top a$$ 
where $a\in\mathbb{S}^1$ is such that
\begin{align*}
    \langle a, x^{1+}\rangle&>0,\\
    \langle a,x\rangle&<0\hspace{1cm}\text{for }x\in \bigcup_{j=2}^N \mathrm{supp}(\mu_0^j).
\end{align*}
(As such, the perceptron component of the vector field vanishes for $2\leqslant i\leqslant N$.)
nodes.statement_short: Choose U so the perceptron acts only near $x^{1+}$.

nodes.name: Feedback W
nodes.statement_short: Choose W(t) to cancel attention at the atom.

nodes.name: Equation (D.6)
nodes.statement: \left(\left\langle a,x^{1+}\right\rangle\right)_+\bm{\mathit{W}}(t){\bf1}+\mathscr{A}_{\bm{\mathit{B}}}\left[\mu^1(t)\right](x^{1+})=x^{1+}.
nodes.label: eq: feedback.W

nodes.name: Other measures cluster
nodes.statement:
Since we now operate on $\mathbb{Q}_1^1$, and the vector field $x\mapsto\bm{\mathit{W}}(\bm{\mathit{U}} x)_+$ does not affect $\mu_0^i$ for $2\leqslant i\leqslant N$, the solution to the Cauchy problem \eqref{eq: cauchy.pb} emanating from $\mu_0^i$ converges weakly to 
a point mass $\updelta_{z^i}$ as $t\to+\infty$, for some $z^i$ lying in $\mathrm{conv}_g \,\mathrm{supp}(\mu^i_0)$ (see \Cref{prop: targets.atoms}, or the arguments of \cite[Theorem 4.1]{geshkovski2023mathematical}).
nodes.statement_short: Other measures cluster to points in their hulls (Prop. 2.1).

nodes.name: Choose B
nodes.statement_short: Choose B with large eigenvalue along $x^{1+}$; reduce to an attention-direction property.

nodes.name: Equation (D.7)
nodes.statement: \mathscr{A}_{\bm{\mathit{B}}}[\mu^1(t)](x)\in sB(x^{1+},C\varepsilon)
nodes.label: eq: attention.set

nodes.name: Attention points to the atom
nodes.statement_short: Show the attention direction stays near $x^{1+}$.

nodes.name: Attention bounded below
nodes.statement:
Consider
    $$\mathscr{C}:=\mathrm{conv }(\mathbb{Q}_1^1).$$ 
For every $\mu\in\mathscr{P}(\mathbb{Q}_1^1)$ and $x\in\mathrm{supp}(\mu)$ one has
$\mathscr{A}_{\bm{\mathit{B}}}[\mu](x)\in\mathscr{C}$ since $\mathscr{A}_{\bm{\mathit{B}}}[\mu](x)$ is a weighted average of the elements of the support of $\mu$. This implies that 
\begin{equation} \|\mathscr{A}_{\bm{\mathit{B}}}[\mu](x)\|\geqslant c
\end{equation}
for some $c>0$ and for every $x\in\mathrm{supp}(\mu)$.
nodes.statement_short: Attention lies in the convex hull, so its norm is bounded below.

nodes.name: Equation (D.8)
nodes.statement: \|\mathscr{A}_{\bm{\mathit{B}}}[\mu](x)\|\geqslant c
nodes.label: eq: low.bound.attention

nodes.name: Direction of attention
nodes.statement_short: Decompose the attention integral; with $\beta=\varepsilon^{-3}$ it points near $x^{1+}$.

nodes.name: Separate the first measure
nodes.statement_short: The first measure clusters near $x^{1+}$, away from the others.

nodes.name: Rotate and induct
nodes.statement_short: Rotate the separated measure out of the way and repeat.

nodes.name: Relabel
nodes.statement:
For convenience, we relabel the measures obtained from the previous step by resetting time: $\mu_0^i=\mu^i(T_2(\eta))$. 
In this last step, we set $\bm{\mathit{V}}\equiv0$, to send the first measure counter-clockwise to $\mathbb{Q}^1_1$ so that it has disjoint support with the other measures, and so that $\langle x^{1+}, e_2\rangle$ is smaller than the infimum of $x\mapsto\langle x, e_2\rangle$ over the supports of all the other measures. This argument can then be repeated for every $i\in[N]$.
nodes.statement_short: Reset time and describe the rotation.

nodes.name: First rotation field
nodes.statement_short: Perceptron field active only on the first measure pointing into the fourth quadrant.

nodes.name: Rotate into the orthant
nodes.statement_short: Move the first measure then back into the orthant below the others.

nodes.name: Supports do not grow
nodes.statement_short: Supports only shrink, so disjointness persists.

nodes.name: Induction
nodes.statement_short: Relabel and repeat for all measures.
